train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29539/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Łódź. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The judge ruled that the application was admissible under Article 29 of the convention.  Łódź Regional Court found that there had been several periods of unjustified inactivity. Court did not examine, however, the period prior to the entry into force of the 2004 Act. Court awarded the applicant 1,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 285 euros (EUR) in just satisfaction. name: Stuart Gray
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, made the application in September 2009. They complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors had led to their father’s death. In each case they alternatively invoked a breach of Articles 8, 13 and 14 of the convention. On 18 December 2012 the application was declared partly inadmissible pursuant to Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4. as being manifestly ill-founded as regards the complaints against the United Kingdom and the complaints under Article 14. The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by ‘Take Care Now’ Dr U. was recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U. had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. He had applied to be admitted to one of the Medical Performers Lists maintained by each of the local PCTs. The Cornwall and Isles of Scilly PCT authorities approved a subsequent application and admitted him to their Performers List in July 2007 without verifying his English language skills. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany where he arrived the following day. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. U. apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment. He said he had confused the opiates and referred to the stress situation he was subject to when making the mistake. The criminal proceedings were instituted against U. in the United Kingdom and Germany. The application was dismissed in May 2008 and U. was allowed to return to work as a locum doctor in Germany. In August 2008 the applicant attended a further hearing before the GMC in London where his suspension from the medical register was confirmed. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the U.K. established as the cause of the death diamorphine poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication and hypertensive heart disease. Cambridgeshire Constabulary, through Interpol London, made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) in March 2008. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany. The Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray pursuant to Article 152 § 2 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure. Cambridgeshire police officers visited Germany on several occasions in the period from July until September 2008 and were provided with assistance by the German police in their investigations against U. The investigations focussed on the authenticity of the certificates U. had submitted to the English health authorities as evidence of his medical qualifications as well as on the question whether U’s treatment of the deceased had amounted to medical malpractice. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital. The expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray's death had been an overdose of diamorphine. He pointed out that notwithstanding the fact that the therapeutical use of diammorphine was in general not permitted in Germany and therefore doctors in Germany were as a rule not trained in its use, U had used it. Cambridgeshire police provided their German counterparts upon request with certain documents for use in the preliminary proceedings conducted against U. in Germany. The expert concluded that U’s treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray's acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. According to a file note by the Bochum public prosecution authorities of 5 November 2008, the German prosecution authorities had informed Cam Bridgeshire Constabulary in reply to a similar request made over the phone that day that they had been obliged by operation of law. On 27 February 2009 an arrest warrant was issued against U. by the Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court, Cambridgeshire. On 12 March 2009 the Colchester Magistrates' Court issued a European Arrest Warrant (”EAW’) against U for allegedly having caused the death of Mr Gray with an overdose of morphine. On the same day, the Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ordered that the preliminary criminal proceedings against U be terminated and applied to the Witten District Court for a penal order (Strafbefehl) to be issued. convicting him of having caused Mr Gray’s death through negligence pursuant to Article 222 of the Criminal Code. U. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment and had thus violated basic principles of the medical profession. U. had not been extradited to Germany. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued the penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U. as applied for by the prosecution authorities. By a decision of the same day, the District Court determined that the probation period for U. was two years starting from the date the Penal order became final. The CPS asked the Ministry of Justice of the Land of North Rhine-Westphalia for information why the EAW had not yet been executed. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. The Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U.’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. The content of these discussions is confidential. Counsel for the second applicant was again granted access to the files in the terminated criminal proceedings against U. in April 2010. Criminal investigations in the United Kingdom were discontinued. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. U. was reprimanded for having disregarded the standards of the medical profession. He committed himself to refrain from practising medicine abroad in the future. The health authorities found that there was nothing to establish that U. would commit a similar error of treatment in Germany or that he lacked the necessary qualifications for practising Medicine. There was no need to suspend or revoke U’s licence to practice medicine in Germany and discontinued the proceedings regarding his fitness to practice. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. The latter returned the verdict that the deceased had been unlawfully killed as a consequence of the inadequate treatment administered by U.D. Subsequent investigations and proceedings were instituted in the United Kingdom following Mr. Gray’s death. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants by consent orders of December 2009, January and August 2010. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cam Bridgeshire PCT.

name: Bahar Yeşilyurt
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15649/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Bahar Yeşilyurt (“the applicant”) was brought before the investigating judge at the Istanbul State Security Court, who ordered her detention on remand. In the subsequent hearings, the court refused to release the applicant on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of evidence. The case against the applicant continued before the Diyarbakır State security Court until 7 May 2004 when, following a constitutional amendment, State Security Courts were abolished. Diyarbakır Assize Court declared its lack of jurisdiction and transferred the applicant's case to the Diyarbak Turkey Juvenile Court. The case file was then transferred to the Batman Assize court. The applicant was acquitted of the charges against her on 4 December 2007. She has not yet received the due amount of compensation for the damage caused by being unjustifiably arrested or detained. According to the information submitted by the applicant, the proceedings are still pending before the Court of Cassation, following her appeal, and she hasn't yet received her due amount. She was awarded 11,881 Turkish liras (TRY) in respect of pecuniary damage and TRY 10,000 for non-pecuniary damages.

name: Rolf Lundevall
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38629/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal in proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant claimed that he had failed to fully state his need of assistance and his additional costs in the original application. On 27 April 1991 he asked the Office, alternatively, to consider his request as a new application and to grant him benefits as from November 1988. On 12 July 1991 the Office found that there was no basis for a review of its earlier decision. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. It considered that the Office’s first decision had been based on insufficient information. The applicant made submissions in response to the Board’s appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative Court of Appeal to hold an oral hearing in the case during which the person in charge of the case at the Office should give evidence. The latter request was granted by a decision of 30 December 1992. The applicant maintained that the Board had failed to adequately explain the reasons for its appeal. He also asked the court to obtain the opinion of a medical expert. The court did not do so, however. By 3 votes to 2, it quashed the County Administrative Court's judgment and confirmed the Office's decision. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) of 12 July 1991. The dissenting judges considered that the applicant was entitled to the disability allowance granted to him by the County Administrative Court and that, for this reason, there were exceptional reasons to change the Office’s decision. Without giving any further reasons, it considered that there had been no basis for a review of the Office's first decision. As an allowance could be given retroactively only for the two years preceding the application, the applicantwas granted an allowance as from October 1994.On 9 October 1996 the applicant made a renewed request for a disability allowance. By a decision of 12 December 1996 the Office found that he had special needs and costs due to his handicap which made him eligible for disability benefits.

name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. Uli Lutz, on 14 June 1982. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government’s memorial was lodged with the registry on 13 November 1986. The applicant informed the Registrar on the same day that he would not be filing a memorial. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by. Mr. Wingerter and Mr. Hohbach for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. He was fined DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14, for “joint responsibility for a road. accident due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation such that a collision was. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz) and Regulations 1(2), 5 and 49. The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) The case was heard in the Heilbronn District Court (Amtsgericht) on 5 February 1981. The District Court stayed the proceedings on the ground that they were time-barred. On 12 August, Mr. Wingerter replied that his client naturally agreed to the stay of proceedings, but not to an order requiring him to bear his own necessary costs and expenses. On 9 December 1980, the Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. On 10 September 1981, the applicant challenged this decision in so far as he had been ordered to bear his own costs and expenses. The court declined to order the Treasury to bear the defendant’s necessary costs. The decision on costs is based on Article 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’ (Gesetz über Ordnungswidrigkeiten) Mr. Lutz had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. Mr Lutz then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), but on 2 February 1982 a bench of three judges refused to entertain the application. In the Constitutional Court, the decisions of the District Court and the Regional Court did not offend the presumption of innocence. The presumption of innocence precluded taking measures against a defendant (Beschuldigter) that amounted in effect to a penalty (Strafe) This rule was not infringed where the necessary costs and expenses of a party who had been proceeded against in respect of a “regulatory offence’ were not awarded against the Treasury in the event of the proceedings being discontinued. The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and. expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with. such. The reasons for the order as to costs in the impugned decisions are therefore rightly confined to the finding that the defendant would most probably have been found guilty.

name: Ludwig Weh
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38544/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 4 July 2002. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1). The Court ruled that the application was not inadmissible on 1 November 2001. The application was dismissed on 1 February 2002. The applicant, Mr W. Weh, was born in 1952 and lives in Bregenz. He was ordered to pay 800 Austrian schillings for exceeding the speed limit by 21 km/h. He did not comply with the anonymous order and the order became invalid. The applicant appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) The panel dismissed the appeal on 15 April 1996. The application was dismissed and the applicant was sentenced to a fine of ATS 900 (with 24 hours' imprisonment in default) The applicant was also ordered to contribute to the costs of the proceedings. The applicant argued that the information submitted by him was sufficiently accurate. The Panel dismissed the applicant's defence, noting that section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act required the registered car owner to disclose the name and address of the driver. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the complaint pursuant to section 33a of the Administrative Court Act (Verwaltungsgerichtshofgesetz) since the amount of the penalty did not exceed ATS 10,000, and no important legal problem was at stake. the applicant was ordered to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings.

name: John Beard
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24882/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two British nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber on 4 February 2000. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. The applicants are gypsies by birth and regard themselves as being Lancashire folk. In 1986 they bought a piece of land, known as Cinderbarrow Malt Kiln, Yealand Redmayne, Carnforth. The site is 0.365 hectares in area, and is positioned in the countryside between the M6 motorway and the London-Carlisle railway line. When they bought it, they stated that it was generally regarded as being an eyesore. They referred to letters from local residents describing the site as having been used for car breaking and tipping rubbish, being littered and infested. The application was for a small close-knit gypsy family site for six caravans. The Government disputed this assertion, stating that local authority records indicate that it was after the applicants had occupied it that complaints were received about its condition. The site is in an area of open countryside, it is undulating pasture land with a few buildings in the locality. It can be seen from a number of public viewpoints, including the canal towpath close at hand, and further afield, from points along Tarn Lane. The application was rejected on the grounds of adverse effect on highway safety and impact on visual amenity. On 17 December 1991, the applicants submitted an appeal to the Secretary of State. Harm caused to the character of the area by using the site for stationing 6 caravans for residential purposes materially outweighs any benefits that may have accrued from [the applicant's] cleaning up operation. The land leads to the A6070 at one end where visibility is significantly below the standards recommended in Planning Policy Guidance Note 13. 14, even allowing for the proximity of the site to Cinderbarrow Cottage. The hedges along the lane obstruct the visibility at bends, alterations in the hedge line along the site would be a help but in my view such alterations would not go far towards improving the overall situation. Lancashire Council's district is designated under the provisions of the Caravan Sites Act 1968, ..., as an area where adequate provision has been made for gypsies residing in, or resorting to the area. The Council's own site at Mellishaw Park has 20 double pitches and can, therefore, accommodate 40 caravans. The larger picture for the County is that, under Policy 11 of the Structure Plan and in the context of residential development, the aim is to provide land for caravan sites for Gypsies within, or close to, the main urban areas. The County Council are actively pursuing the provision of 3 further sites, none of which are in Lancaster. The applicants were offered places on an authorised site, Mellishaw Park, which they turned down for strong personal reasons. In May 1992, the first applicant received serious injury, being beaten with a baseball bat and being showered with glass as his car was smashed. In June 1993, they applied for planning permission for a smaller gypsy site which would consist of one mobile home and a transit pitch. On 19 July 1993, their application was refused and they appealed against this decision. On 25 January 1994, the appeal was dismissed again, and on 7 June 1994, a public local inquiry was held. In July 1991, during the period when [the first applicant] was clearing up the appeal site prior to moving onto it in August, the Council say there were 21 vacancies on authorised sites. The use of the site for the stationing of a caravan and the addition of a second would “seriously harm the character and appearance of the surrounding area’ Lancaster District has been designated under the provisions of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 as an area where adequate provision has been made for gypsies residing in or resorting to the area. The current level of authorised provision within the district is 100 caravan pitches of which 20 pitches are on a council-owned site. Surveys taken during 1993 show that an average of 29 vacancies existed each month on private sites in the district. The applicants were convicted of failing to comply with the enforcement notice and were fined GBP 300. The applicants appeared once more in the magistrates' court charged with failing to comply with the enforcement notice. The applicants elected to be tried in Preston Crown Court by judge and jury. At a hearing on 8 December, the applicants were directed by the judge that they had no alternative but to plead guilty as they did not have a defence to the charges. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, inter alia, endorsing the judge's finding that: “Subsection 3 [of the Town and Country Planning Act 1996] is not concerned with a balance of social factors. It is not. concerned with the policy issues as arise in relation to the circumstances in which gypsies live.” The applicants say they have been unable to find alternative accommodation elsewhere. The application was refused and the applicants ordered to pay the Council's costs. Only one of the sites has been designated as official gypsy site but is still inhabited mostly by non-gypsies. The applicants say that these sites are largely seasonal for tourists and that gypsies were not welcome. According to the 1999 statistics of the Department of the Environment however, the number of authorised private sites had increased by six (from 68 to 74) The number of public sites had decreased by the same number (from 25 to 19) The applicants would only have had to wait 4–6 months for a vacancy to occur on the official site in the district. The total number of unauthorised encampments in the area had almost doubled from 11 to 21. However, the number of people living in encampments was still lower than in 2010. The number of campers had fallen from 1,700 to 1,800. The most common type of camp is a tent, which is made up of around 50 people. Some campers live in the middle of the road, while others are on the edge of the street. There are also reports of people sleeping in the open in the streets at night, in the early hours of the morning and during the day. The campers are said to be caused by people living under the influence of drugs or alcohol.

Unauthorised encampments in the area had almost doubled from 11 to 21. However, the total number of unauthorised camps had remained the same. The number of encampments had increased by two per cent from 11, to 21, to make up for the decline in the number of people living in the encampments. The increase in encampments was down to an increase in people living around the camp, which had also increased by one per cent since the start of the year, according to the Department of the Environment and Climate Change ( DCCC) The DCCE has been working with the DCCCC to address the problem, which has led to a rise in the amount of people camping in the region.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24882/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two British nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided in February 2000. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Drabble and Mr Pannick. On 29 November 2000, Mr Makarczyk, who was unable to take part in further consideration of the case, was replaced by Mr Bonello (Rules 24 § 5 (b) and 28). The applicants regard themselves as being Lancashire folk. The site is 0.365 hectares in area, and is positioned in the countryside between the M6 motorway and the London-Carlisle railway line. When the applicants bought it, they stated that it was generally regarded as being an eyesore. In August 1991, the applicants moved onto the site and on 17 September 1991 they applied for planning permission for a small close-knit gypsy family site for six caravans. On 18 October 1991, they were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court for being on the land unlawfully. They were convicted and fined 75 pounds sterling (GBP) They spent two years cleaning it up and developing it. with rats. The Government disputed this assertion, stating that local authority records indicate that it was after the applicants had occupied it that complaints were received about its condition. They stated that the land was previously used for grazing and growing crops. Planning permission for the appeal site was granted for six caravans to be built on land near Cinderbarrow Cottage. The land was overgrown until 1990 or thereabouts and is not overgrown now. The site leads to the A6070 at one end where visibility is significantly below the standards recommended in Planning Policy Guidance Note 13. 14. The hedges along the lane obstruct the visibility at bends, alterations in the hedge line along the site would be a help but in my view such alterations would not go far towards improving the overall situation. The first applicant says he uses only the Tarn Lane junction, but I consider that others may well use the other junctions either because of convenience or because they do not appreciate the different standards. The Lancashire Council's district is designated under the provisions of the Caravan Sites Act 1968. There are 5 permanent gypsy sites in the County, including the one at Mellishaw Park. The County Council are actively pursuing the provision of 3 further sites, none of which are in Lancaster. The Council say that provision has been made over and above that which led to the area being designated. Fourteen additional residential pitches and 4 pitches for touring caravans have been provided on 4 private sites ... The Council's own site at Mellistaw Park has 20 double pitches and can, therefore, accommodate 40 caravan. The applicants tried unsuccessfully to find an alternative site both in the Lancashire City Council area and in the nearby Cumbria Council area. They were offered places on an authorised site, Mellishaw Park, which they turned down for strong personal reasons. The applicants were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court and given a conditional discharge for one year, which would expire on 28 May 1994. They applied for planning permission for a smaller gypsy site which would consist of one mobile home and a transit pitch. On 19 July 1993, their application was refused and they appealed against this decision. On 25 January 1994, the appeal was dismissed. On 21 December 1993, a public local inquiry was held. Lancaster District has been designated under the provisions of the Caravan Sites Act 1968, as amended, as an area where adequate provision has been made for gypsies residing in or resorting to the area. The current level of authorised provision within the district is 100 caravan pitches of which 20 pitches are on a council-owned site. Surveys taken during 1993 show that an average of 29 vacancies existed each month on private sites in the district. The applicants were convicted of failing to comply with the enforcement notice and were fined GBP 300 plus costs in January 1995. The applicants elected to be tried in Preston Crown Court by judge and jury. The applicants were directed by the judge that they had no alternative but to plead guilty as they did not have a defence to the charges. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, inter alia, endorsing the judge's finding that: “Subsection 3 [of the Town and Country Planning Act 1996] is not concerned with a balance of social factors.” The case was remitted to the Crown Court judge, who took the view that there was “powerful mitigation” and sentenced the applicants to a fine of GBP 150 and GBP 100 costs. The Commission was set up to help gypsies find alternative accommodation. The first applicant was committed to prison for three months in November 1997. The application was refused and the applicants were ordered to pay the Council's costs. The applicants have since vacated their land and are currently without a fixed address. The Commission has been unable to find alternative accommodation and has been left with no choice but to seek a new home. It has been described as a ‘victory of the human spirit’. It is the first of a series of cases that will be heard by the Commission in the coming months. The case is expected to last until the end of the year. The total number of unauthorised encampments in the area had almost doubled from 11 to 21. However, the number of people living in encampments had also almost doubled in the last year. The number of homeless people has almost doubled as a result of the increase in the encampments. The increase in homeless people is estimated to be around 20,000 a year. This is a rise of more than 30 per cent in the past five years, according to the Department of Health and Social Security (DSS). The increase is due to a rise in the number and location of encampments, as well as the amount of people sleeping in tents and makeshift shelters.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ consent, the case was dismissed. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The Ankara Assize Court decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time-barred. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application admissible and declared it to be a criminal case. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice.

name: Halit Tendik
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the period of their detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement. They were accused of involvement in separatist activities and being members of, and aiding and abetting, the PKK. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The case was assigned to newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants were born in 1972, 1969, 1977 and 1947 respectively. The case-file was transferred to the State Security Court on 2 June 1997. The first and second applicants were sentenced to life in prison. The third was sentenced to 15 years in prison and the fourth to 12 years. The decision was quashed on 29 November 2001 on the grounds of a breach of the right of defence. The case was then handed back to the Court of Cassation. The court has since ruled that the case should not have been transferred to a different court. The second case was dismissed and the third case was dropped. The fourth case was decided in favour of the applicants and the sentence was commuted to 12 months in jail.

The case originated in an application (no. 23188/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the period of their detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement, that the criminal proceedings brought against them were not concluded within areasonable time, and that they did not have an effective remedy at their disposal under domestic law in that respect. The Court decided to communicate the application on 2 June 2004. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. This case was assigned to newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case-file was transferred to the State Security Court on 2 June 1997. On 8 January 1999, the first and second applicants were sentenced to death. The third was sentenced to life in prison and the fourth to fifteen years' imprisonment. On 29 November 2001, the Court of Cassation quashed the lower court’s decision to sentence the applicants to death and the sentence was commuted to 16 years in prison. The case- file was then transferred back to the state security court. The decision was then quashed again on 29 November 2002. The last hearing on the case was held on 17 December 2003, and the sentences were again commuted. The sentence was finally quashed on 18 December 2002.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34619/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated as the Tax Authority's decisions on taxes and tax surcharges had been enforced prior to a court determination of the dispute. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 September 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Thörnhammar and Ms Kalmerborn. The Tax Authority increased the applicant's liability to income tax by 286,859 Swedish kronor (SEK) The additional taxes levied on the applicant, including interest and surcharges, totalled SEK 1,020,300, of which SEK 161,261 were surcharges. As he risked being declared bankrupt before his tax liability had been determined by the courts, he also requested a stay of execution in respect of the amounts assessed. The amounts relating to value-added tax and employer's contributions were payable on 5 January 1996 and those relating to incomeTax on 10 April 1996. The Tax Authority considers that the prerequisites laid down in section 49, subsection 1(2) or (3), of the Tax Collection Act [Uppbördslagen, 1953:272] have been fulfilled. Tax Authority found that applicant's ability to pay is open to serious doubt. Tax Authority rejected the applicant's request for a stay of execution, as no security had been furnished. The applicant appealed against those decisions to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm. Both claims rested on the contention that it would be unreasonable and amount to a violation of Article 6 of the Convention for enforcement proceedings to be instituted against the applicant without a court having first determined whether he had any liability to pay the amounts involved. On 21 May 1997 the Administrative Court of Appeal in Stockholm refused him leave to appeal against the County administrative Court's judgments. On 3 November 1998 the Supreme Administrative Court refused his appeal. The applicant's tax liability as of 22 March 1996 amounted to SEK 653,144. That amount included SEK 89,323, plus 6% in penalties for late payment, in tax surcharges. The only property owned by the applicant was some vehicles, but of insufficient value to cover the debt. The applicant appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) on 18 June 1996. The appeal was dismissed. Leave to appeal against the appellate court's decision was refused by the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) on18 September 1996. In so doing it had regard to the fact that, under section 103 of the Tax Collection Act, the applicant was under an obligation to pay the debt and had to be considered insolvent as he had been found to have no distrainable assets. The whole debt became statute-barred on 31 December 2001, at the end of the fifth year following the day it became due. The applicant was sentenced by the District Court to ten months' imprisonment for tax fraud (skattebedrägeri) and a bookkeeping offence (bokföringsbrott) The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 16 November 1998. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 4 March 1999. Further proceedings concerning the taxes and tax surcharges concerning the applicant were referred to the County Administrative Court for determination in September 2001. By a letter of 5 September 2001 the applicant requested an oral hearing at which it was proposed that certain witnesses would give evidence. Tax Authority had good reason to make discretionary tax assessments based on the information obtained during the audit. Administrative Court informed the applicant that it did not find a hearing necessary and ordered him to make his final observations in the case in writing. The applicant has appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, where the dispute is at present pending. The County Administrative Court made extensive references to the judgments of the Supreme Court of 29 November 2000 and the Supreme Administrative court of 15 December 2000 (see paragraphs 51-55 below) It considered that there had been sufficient reasons to impose the surcharges in question and that no legal basis for remitting them had been shown.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor’s fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time. The Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board claimed that the applicant had not participated in the test series for quality checking of laboratory parameters in 1997, and refused to pay for the tests. The application was dismissed in 1999 but the applicant appealed against that decision to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommission). The applicant lives in St Oswald and has an individual contract (Einzelvertrag) with the Lower Austrian health insurance board. The applicant filed an application for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) in 1999. The decision was dated 24 August 1999, and was served on the applicant on 7 July 2000. On 27 November 2000 the Constitutional Court set aside the decision for violation of the right to a fair hearing. The applicant was summoned to another hearing by a newly composed Regional Appeals Commission on 26 November 2003. During that hearing the entire subject was examined anew. On 15 December 2004 the applicant complained to the. Constitutional Court claiming that the Regional Appeals. Commission lacked independence and impartiality. The former rejected the applicant’s complaint in a decision of 27 September 2005. The decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The mere fact that the assessors were members of Regional Medial Associations or Regional Health Insurance Boards which had provisions with the same content in their general agreements, did not suffice to cast doubt on the independence and impartiality of the Regional Appeals Commission. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal on 26 November 2005 and the case was heard before the High Court on 28 November. The hearing was adjourned until 3 December 2005. It took place in London and the hearing was held in Edinburgh. The case was referred to the Supreme Court of Justice. The appeal was decided by the court of Appeal and the decision was delivered on 3 January 2005.

On 7 May 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) An amendment to the Social Insurance Act (Allgemeines Sozialversicherungsgesetz) entered into force on 1 September 2002. It provided for changes in the composition of, inter alia, the Regional Appeals Commission. On 17 May 1999 the applicant filed an application for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag), requesting a decision on his submission of 5 October 1998. The decision was dated 24 August 1999, and was served on the applicant on 7 July 2000. The applicant complained about this decision to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Constitutional Court set aside the decision for violation of the right to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal. The decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The mere fact that the assessors were members of Regional Medial Associations or Regional Health Insurance Boards did not suffice to cast doubt on the independence and impartiality of the Regional Appeals Commission. The decision was made by the European Court of Human Rights on 27 November 2005 and appealed to the High Court of Justice. The appeal was dismissed on 28 November 2005, and the appeal was upheld on 26 November 2005 by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The High Court ruled that the Commission was not impartial unless special circumstances, for instance the fact that one member of the Commission had been involved in the negotiation of the general agreements, gave rise to legitimate doubts about that member's independence.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 16969/90) against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 May 1990 by an Irish citizen, Mr Joseph Keegan. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 November 1993. The Registrar consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the procedure. The Court heard addresses by Sir Basil Hall, Ms Browne and Mr Gleeson as well as replies to questions put by several of its members. The proceedings before the Circuit Court were heard by a jury of nine judges. The decision was returned in favour of the applicant and the adoption proceedings were dismissed. The case was heard by the Judge of Appeal for the European Court of Human Rights. Father applied for custody and guardianship of his child. Circuit Court appointed applicant guardian and awarded him custody. High Court found applicant was a fit person to be appointed guardian and that there were no circumstances involving the welfare of the child which required that the father’s rights be denied. Father and prospective adopters appealed to Supreme Court for opinion. Court ruled in favour of the applicant, giving him custody of his son. Court of Appeal ruled that the application could not proceed without the consent of the mother and the child's guardian (see paragraph 19 below). Court of appeals ruled that Mr Justice Barron was correct to take into account that the child had been placed for adoption. Chief Justice Finlay said the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act as conferring on the natural father a right to be a guardian. The first and paramount consideration in the exercise of the court’s discretion was the welfare of the child, and the blood link between child and father as merely one of the many relevant factors which may be viewed by the court as relevant to that question. He concluded that: “... regard should not be had to the objective of satisfying the wishes and desires of the father to be involved in the guardianship of his child’” The extent and character of the rights which accrue arising from the relationship of a father to a child to whose mother he is not married must vary very greatly indeed, depending on the circumstances. The High Court resumed its examination of the case in early 1990. It heard, inter alia, the evidence of a consultant child psychiatrist who considered that the child would suffer short-term trauma if moved to the applicant’s custody. In the longer term she would be more vulnerable to stress and be less able to cope with it. The matter was then referred back to the High Court for the case to be decided in light of this interpretation. In his judgment of 9 February 1990 Mr Justice Barron recalled that the applicant wished bona fide to have custody of his daughter and that he felt the existence of an emotional bond. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living. An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child. The father's desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account. In these circumstances, the welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. Accordingly the application for relief must be refused.‘The quality of welfare likely to be achieved with the prospective adopters would not be to an important extent better than that likely to. be achieved by custody with the father. That being so, his wish and desire. to be in charge of and enjoy thesociety of his son is not. a factor to be taken into account’

name: Abdurrahman Şiray
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29724/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Mr Abdurrahman Şiray, is a Turkish national who was born in 1972 and lives in Siirt. He was arrested in Mardin and taken into police custody with three other individuals on suspicion of acting as a courier for an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK/KADEK. The applicant denied any affiliation with the illegal organisation and contested F.A.’s allegations. He also explained that he had been carrying a false identity card as he was an army deserter. The applicant was brought before the Nusaybin Public Prosecutor on 23 June 2003 and remanded in pre-trial custody. His co-accused, F.A., also made statements before the public prosecutor and the magistrates’ court. The applicant denied all charges against him, as well as retracting the statements he had made before the police. He asserted that those statements had been extracted from him under duress and that he had no way of knowing whether they had been translated into Turkish accurately. State Security Courts were abolished by Law no. 5190 of 16 June 2004 after the applicant’s lawyer argued that the only piece of evidence found against him was F.F.A.'s statements made during the preliminary investigation. The Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 22 December 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. The case was re-examined in view of the recent legislative changes. The new Criminal Code which had entered into force on 1 June 2005 (Law no. 5237) had provisions which would be more favourable for the applicant. In delivering its judgment, the first-instance court mainly relied on the statements made by F.A. in respect of the applicant during the preliminary investigation stage.

The case stems from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 6 June 2008. The applicant, Mr Abdurrahman Şiray, is a Turkish national who was born in 1972 and lives in Siirt. On 20 June 2003 the applicant, who is of Kurdish origin, was arrested in Mardin and taken into police custody with three other individuals on suspicion of acting as a courier for an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK/KADEK. Before his questioning the applicant signed a form which explained the rights of arrested persons. He was informed of the charges against him and his right to remain silent. The applicant was brought before the Nusaybin Public Prosecutor on 23 June 2003 and remanded in pre-trial custody. On the same day the applicant’s co-accused, F.A., also made statements before the public prosecutor and the Magistrates’ Court. On 7 July 2003 the Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court filed an indictment accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK. On 19 August 2003 the applicant informed the court that he did not have sufficient knowledge of Turkish to follow the hearings. The court bailiff, who spoke Kurdish, was therefore appointed as interpreter. At the hearing, the applicant denied the charges against him, but confirmed that the statements he had made in police custody were accurate. The case was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court in view of the recent legislative changes. The applicant was again found guilty and sentenced to four years and six months in prison. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court on 22 December 2008. The case was re-examined on 14 February 2006 under the new Criminal Code which had entered into force on 1 June 2005 (Law no. 5237) The applicant appealed the original conviction, but the appeal was upheld on 11 May 2006. The application was dismissed on 17 May 2008, and the case was dismissed again on 17 July 2008.

name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. On 16 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Saint-Didier-au-Mont-d’Or. The case involved a third-party payment system. In order to be fully reimbursed by the social security scheme for the health care provided, Clinique du Parc had to wait for the invoice from the prosthesis supplier, which meant a delay of several days, if not weeks. The applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court. The prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty, and that it lacked jurisdiction to examine the claims of the civil parties. It was decided that the offence was not made out and the applicant was accordingly acquitted. The Principal Public Prosecutor lodged an appeal against the judgment on 20 April 2001. The applicant was found guilty of the offence of fraud and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. In a judgment of 25 June 2003 the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal, holding in particular that the two-month time-limit for an appeal was not in breach of Article 6. The Lyon Court of Appeal upheld the judgment appealed against in so far as it had declared that the prosecution of the offense of professional conspiracy had lapsed by virtue of an amnesty.

name: Aziz Aydın Arslan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28353/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Aziz Aydın Arslan (‘the applicant’), was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank. In 1991 he was appointed to the post of deputy director in charge of credit cards. An investigation was carried out as a result of fraudulent acts in the Topkapı branch of the Bank. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 19 March 2007. Criminal proceedings were brought against the director of the Topkapı branch of the Bank and three other persons for having committed a fraud. The applicant and the Bank intervened in these proceedings as a third party. On 9 July 1999 the Bakırköy Assize Court in Istanbul convicted the director and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment for having abused his duty. It however acquitted the other accused. On 29 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the above judgment. On 31 December 2004 the Bak   Assize Court terminated the criminal proceedings against the director since they were time-barred.

The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Istanbul. In 1988 the applicant was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank. The applicant and the Bank intervened in these proceedings as a third party. The appeal was dismissed again on 29 July 2006. The judge said that the director had not committed a fraud and that the appeal should be dismissed again.

name: Wiesław Chodecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. Wiesław Chodecki (‘the applicant’) was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife in June 1994. The applicant was remanded in custody until 12 August 1994 in connection with the investigation against him. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was detained on remand in Sosnowiec, Poland. He was convicted as charged and sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed the conviction and the case was re-examined. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The hearing scheduled for 17 February 1998 was adjourned. The court made reference to the reasonableness of the suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It stressed the serious nature of that offence and the necessity to consider further evidence. The applicant’s lawyer contested the reasonableness of the charge against his client, maintaining that it was solely based on presumptive evidence. The Katowice Regional Court again convicted the applicant of homicide and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. The applicant challenged that decision before a court which did not have the necessary jurisdiction. The matter was transferred to the Katowiced Court of Appeal, which on 25 February 1999 dismissed both of his appeals. On 6 March 2000 the Supreme Court dismissed that appeal. The application was dismissed by the Court of cassation and the appeal was dismissed. The case was settled at the High Court of Justice in the city of Bratislava.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. The applicant was arrested in July 1994. The Sosnowiec District Court ordered that two psychiatric reports be obtained in order to establish the applicant’s criminal responsibility. The prosecutor asked the court to hear evidence from 38 witnesses. The trial court held hearings on 12 January, 16 March, 21 March, 28 March, 1 June, 8 June, 20 June, 12 October and 12 December 1995, as well as on 28 March 1996. The court convicted the applicant as charged, and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 30 May 1996 the applicant appealed. The Katowice Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. On 24 September 1998 the Katowice Regional Court gave judgment. It again convicted the applicant of homicide and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment. The court deducted from the sentence the period spent by the applicant in detention. On 26 November 1998 the applicant’s lawyer appealed against that decision. On 11 January 1999 the matter was transferred to theKatowice Court of Appeal, which on 25 February 1999 dismissed both of his appeals. The applicant then lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court concerning the conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court dismissed that appeal on 6 March 2000. The case is still pending at the European Court of Human Rights.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17730/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: J. Peter
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The case was dismissed on 3 June 2013 after the applicant complained about the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (no. 1 BvR 170/06) with the Federal Constitutional Court in 2006. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) was passed. The applicant was served with a copy of the decision on 13 July 2010 and requested a decision to the same effect on 1 December 2009. On 11 June 2010 a three-judge panel decided not to review the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The applicant complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long. He pointed out that his case could not be considered a particularly difficult one. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 cases did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the constitutional complaint. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. A new judge rapporteur had stepped in at the end of his predecessor's term of office and his predecessor had had to finish cases of higher priority than that of the applicant. In hindsight the present case could have been decided without reference to the ‘pilot case’ The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 2 amended the Federal Constitutional Court Act as follows: “Section 97a (1) Any person who, as the result of the unreasonable length of proceedings, experiences a disadvantage as a participant in those proceedings, shall be afforded reasonable compensation” Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing. Complaint must be admissible 12 months at the earliest after the case has been lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. The decision is not subject to appeal.’’ ‘‘In a departure from the general transitional provision under section 23 of the Remedy Act, the complaint had to be lodged by 3 June 2012 at the latest'’ '‘It was not necessary to raise a complaint of. undue delay (Verzögerungsrüge) prior to filing a complaint claiming compensation'

The case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant, Mr J. Peter, entered into a civil partnership with Mr Peter, né V., on 5 October 2001. In September 2002 the applicant applied for a survivor’s pension to the German Pension Fund (Bundesversicherungsanstalt für Angestellte), a public-law corporation. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat. The applicant's civil partnership had not lasted longer than a year, which would have led to statutory exclusion from the benefit even for married couples. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. On 20 January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (no. 1 BvR 170/06) with the Federal Constitutional Court. In its reasoning the panel explained that the complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. On 7 December 2011 the Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) was to be introduced. The applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long, even taking the position and function of the Federal Constitutional Court into account. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, the judge maintained that it had been in the applicant's best interest to wait for the court's ruling in the 2007 case. Subsequently, it became clear that the 2007 cases did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicants' complaint. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Citing Gast and Popp v. Germany (no. 29357/95, ECHR 2000‑II), the court noted that a chronic backlog of cases in the constitutional courts could not justify the excessive length of proceedings. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The court further explained that it was in the nature of constitutional court proceedings that chronological case management was of subordinate importance. A new judge rapporteur had stepped in at the end of his predecessor's term of office and his predecessor had to finish cases of higher priority than that of the applicant. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. The decision is not subject to appeal.’’ ‘The complaint is admissible twelve months at the earliest after the case has been lodged with the Federal Constitutional Court’ '’ The complaint is not required to be made within one month of receipt of the reasons for the complaint. It is not necessary to make the complaint before the court before filing a complaint claiming compensation.

name: İzzet Belge
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50171/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression. On 7 July 2014 the complaint concerning the applicant’s right of expression was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr İzzet Belge (”the applicant”), on 10 September 2009. The Cizre Criminal Court held nine hearings on the merits of the case and obtained a report by an expert on the video-recordings of the gathering of 5 September 2005, which stated that the applicant had made a speech to a crowd. The applicant denied the allegation that he praised an illegal organisation in his speech and that he had not intended to disseminate propaganda. The case was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court and the applicant made a statement to it on 8 May 2007. He contended that he. had not disseminated propaganda during his speech but had only thanked those who had worked for peace and had condemned Abdullah Öcalan’s solitary confinement. The applicant's speech is interrupted by boos and the slogan ‘Barışa uzanan eller kırılsın’ (‘May those hands which aim to damage peace be broken’). We were taken into police custody because of our democratic reaction to the search order. We were kept in police custody for one night and then taken before a court. The court released us. However, it took a decision to place me under judicial control. I have to go to give my signature every Monday and I am banned from travelling abroad. Those who are against unity and solidarity in this country and those who do not want this country to reach modernity, that is to say, who obtain an unjustified gain out of this war. Demonstrators waved yellow, red and green pieces of cloth and carried photographs of Abdullah Öcalan. Some of the applicant’s co-accused were seen chanting slogans or carrying photographs of the Kurdish leader. The demonstration organised by Tuhay-Der will contribute to peace because a one-month ceasefire has been declared. We condemn with contempt those who obstructed the peace march. We want peace and we will continue to struggle for peace. I thank you all. You can disperse now in silence ...““We want an end to the crying of the mothers of guerrillas and soldiers in this country. On 19 February 2008 the Diyarbakır Assize Court delivered its judgment. The court noted that those who disseminated propaganda in favour of the PKK were expressing their support and approval for the PKK, whose methods were those of terrorism and violence. As a result, the first-instance court convicted the applicant of disseminating propaganda in. favour of a terrorist organisation under section 7. r.                                                                 “The PKK is the people. The people are here.” (“Şırnak ovası PKK’nin yuvası”) On 13 July 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the Diyarbakır Assize Court’s judgment. The court also ordered that Article 53 §§ 1, 2 and 3 of the Criminal Code should apply in respect of the applicant (see paragraph 20 below). The applicant was sentenced to ten months’ imprisonment, but was released on bail. The appeal was rejected on 14 July 2011. The case was heard at the Supreme Court of Justice in Istanbul, which found the applicant guilty of a crime for which he was found guilty by a jury. The appeals process was adjourned until later this year, when it was expected that the judge would rule on the appeal.

name: Wacław Płoski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was then assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. In a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court’s decision on the case is published here as a result of a request from the applicant. The application was accompanied by the statement of a prison officer who supported the applicant’s request. In. terms: “I kindly ask you to grant me leave, on the basis of the telegram received on 3.7.94, [to attend] the funeral of my mother Płoska Stefania, address Bełchatów 67-400, Osiedle Dolnośląskie, Blok 225 – who died.” The application was rejected by the Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court on 4 July 1994. On 6 August 1994 the applicant made an application for leave to attend the funeral. of his father. The application was accompanied by the statement of a prison officer who confirmed that the applicant’s “behaviour was beyond reproach” and that he “stayed in touch with his wife and children” The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society. The accused Wacław Płoski is a habitual offender within the meaning of Article 60 § 2 of the Criminal Code.” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. The applicant was released from prison on 27 February 1996.

The case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant applied for leave to attend the funeral of his mother on 3 July 1994. The application was accompanied by the statement of a prison officer who supported the applicant’s request. On 4 July 1994 the Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused the permission to grant the applicant leave considering that he “was a habitual offender whose return to the prison cannot be guaranteed” On 6 August 1994 the applicant made an application to attend his father's funeral. He wrote: “I kindly ask you to grant me a compassionate leave because my father Wacław Płoski has died. The funeral will take place on 8.08.1994 and I would like to attend it and to pay last respects to him” Wacław Płoski applied for leave to attend the funeral of his father. Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused permission to grant the applicant leave. The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. He was released from prison on 27 February 1996. He has never been allowed to attend his mother and father’s funerals either alone or under police escort. He is currently serving a sentence of two years and four months.
