name: Royce Darnell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15058/89) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 2 December 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The applicant, Dr Royce Darnell, has been unemployed since the Trent Regional Health Authority (‘the RHA’) terminated his employment as a consultant microbiologist and Director of the Public Health Laboratory in Derby. The case concerns the length of time that proceedings relating to this dismissal have taken. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Baker for the Government, by Mr Loucaides for the Commission and by Ms Hampson for the applicant, as well as replies to its questions. The decision was made by the President of the European Court of Human Rights. Dr Darnell was dismissed on three months' notice with effect from 19 August 1984. A professional committee was appointed in accordance with paragraph 190 of the Terms and Conditions of Service of Hospital Medical and Dental Staff. The applicant challenged the fairness of the procedure leading to the Secretary of State’s decision. The High Court granted a declaration that this decision was invalid and indicated that the Secretary. of State should reconsider the matter. The Secretary of. State did not appeal. The paragraph 190 procedure has since been replaced by a new procedure which incorporates time-limits into the various stages of an appeal to the secretary of State against dismissal. Dr Darnell was dismissed by the Department of Health and Social Security in 1988. He had appealed his dismissal to the Secretary of State and the Industrial Tribunal. A pre-hearing assessment took place on 6 February 1989 in which the Tribunal determined that a hearing could take place with no cost consequences to the applicant. In its reserved decision of 23 February 1990, the Tribunal held that the dismissal of the applicant was not unfair. An appeal against the striking out was dismissed in 1990. The applicant’s appeal to the Employment Appeal Tribunal was dismissed on 8 April 1993. He complained under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention that the “civil process’ had been prejudiced. The Commission declared the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings admissible and dismissed the remainder of his application. In its report of 13 May 1992, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) (unanimously) The full text of the Commission's opinion and of the concurring opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment.“ proceedings taken against him which led to the final termination of his employment took an unreasonable length of time; he also alleged that the Secretary of State and the RHA had followed a procedure which was neither fair nor public.

name: Maciej Zys-Kowalski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 70213/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) Four Polish nationals, Mr Maciej Zys-Kowalski, Mrs Danuta Kowalska, Mr Krzysztof Kowalksi and Ms Marta KowALksi (‘the applicants’), made the application on 10 May 2000. The application was finally dismissed on 21 December 2001. The appeal was dismissed in March 2002 by the Supreme Court of Poland. The case is still pending at the Polish Supreme Court.

name: Adnan Levent Çamlar
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. The Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release in 1998. On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6. 1 and 3(d) were communicated to the Government and the. remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar, was represented by Mr A. Cangı, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The applicant was accused of trafficking illegal drugs in Turkey. He was placed on remand in absentia in 1997. In 1999 he was released pending trial. In 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. The court rejected this request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case in view of the information already available concerning the proceedings in the United Kingdom. The applicant was acquitted on 3 December 1998. In March 2003 he was sentenced to 15 years in prison, but was released on appeal on 15 July 2003. The judge sitting on the İzmir State Security Court hearing the applicant's case was replaced by a civilian judge. The applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment and a fine in March 2003. He appealed against that judgment, saying he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. In June 2005, the applicant requested the reassessment of his case and the application of the more favourable clauses in the new Code. The higher court indicated that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom. On 9 April 2009 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and heard the submissions of the applicant’s lawyer. Finally, the higher court upheld the judgment.

On 24 June 2013 the complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of. the Convention concerning the independence and impartiality of the İzmir State Security Court and the applicant’s. inability to examine or have examined witnesses were communicated to the Government. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was charged with the trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. He was released pending trial in 1998. In 2003 he requested his acquittal. The application was rejected on the basis of information about the proceedings in the United Kingdom. He is married and has a son and a daughter, both of whom are Turkish nationals. He also has a daughter and a son-in-law who are Turkish citizens. He currently lives in the US and works for a law firm in Washington, D.C. The case was heard by a military judge before a civilian judge. Finally, on 9 April 2009, the higher court upheld the conviction of the � zmir Assize Court with a minor procedural correction.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the convention. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant was born in 1947 and is homosexual. In 1994 it was discovered that he was infected with the HIV virus. He had transmitted the virus to a 19-year-old man with whom he had sexual contact in 1990. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The court's record of the applicant’s statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships.” The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital; the police accordingly took him there on 16 March 1995. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. The owner of the farm hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The applicant had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. He had lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations. He used to go shopping once a day, usually for beer, and [the witness] would estimate that he had drunk between four and six cans of beer every day. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant returned to Stockholm. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. In his opinion the applicant suffers from a paranoid personality disorder and from alcohol abuse. He is considered to be completely devoid of any sense of being ill and also lacks awareness. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation are deemed to have not yet completely vanished. On 23 April 1999 the County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease. The Court has not been convinced that [the applicant] is not misusing alcohol and finds that he is likely to be unable to control his sexual behaviour. The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [The applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued and that this entails a risk of the infection spreading.” On 12 June 1999 the applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal, before which he relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, the following: “The opinions resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [ the applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol” The applicant had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. He was fully aware that he was carrying the HIV virus and was careful to stress that he is not afraid to die. His attitude towards medication against the HIV infection was negative. In conclusion, C.G. found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder, and that, judging from previous information, the applicant suffered from misuse of alcohol but not from alcohol dependency. The Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger.Reger) Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court, which referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical Officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the. further involuntary placement in isolation. ingsrätten) on 5 October 1999. He was fully aware that he was carrying the HIV virus and was careful to stress that he wasn't afraid to die. His attitude towards medication against the HIV infection was negative. The Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger. Reger). In conclusion, C.G. found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder, and that, judging from previous information, the applicant suffered from misuse of alcohol but not from alcohol dependency. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999. An application was turned down by the County Administrative Court on 12 December 2001. The application referred to the fact that the applicants whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the appeal has been accepted, but that there are no grounds for his further involuntary placement in isolation. The applicant's whereabouts have been known since 2002, but the competent county medical officer has made the assessment that there is no grounds to place him in further isolation.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42967/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion. By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Maissau. He was a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in Austria, within which he assumed the function of a preacher or “regular pioneer” (Prediger, allgemeiner Pionier) The applicant appealed against that order, claiming in particular that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. On 26 March 1998 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungs-gerichtshof) dismissed the applicant's complaint. It noted that the applicant had solely complained about section 24(3) of the Military Service Act in conjunction with the 1998 Act on the Legal Status of Registered Religious Communities. It referred to an earlier decision by which it had found that the obligation to perform military or civilian service raised no concerns as regards compliance with Article 9 of the Convention. The applicant was a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in Austria. In 1998 the Lower Austrian Military Authority issued another conscription order for an examination of his fitness to perform military service. He lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. The applicant filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted. On 1 February 2000 the applicant joined the ‘Religious Order of the Witnesses’ (Orden der Sondervollzeitdiener der Zeugen Jehovas), where he lived and worked as a preacher. In February 2001 he left the order and continued to work as a preached and deacon.

The case originated in an application (no. 42967/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 1 February 2005. The case was brought by Mr Philemon Löffelmann, a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in Austria. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) in 1996. He requested it to repeal the wording ‘recognised religious societies’ in section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 26 March 1998 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint. It noted that the applicant had solely complained about section 24 (3) in conjunction with the 1998 Act on the Legal Status of Registered Religious Communities (Bundesgesetz über die Rechtspersönlichkeit von religiösen Bekenntnisgemeinschaften – hereafter referred to as the “1998 Act”) On 14 May 1998 the Lower Austrian Military Authority issued another conscription order for an examination of the applicant’s fitness to perform military service. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. He submitted in particular that by virtue of the 1998 Act, the Jehovah's Witnesses had been granted the status of a “registered religious community’. However, the ten-year period for a successful application for recognition under the Recognition Act (Anerkennungsgesetz) lacked objective justification, he said. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. Subsequently, the applicant filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector, which was granted.

The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits. By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court's decision has been published in full in the German edition of this article. The Austrian edition has been released in the English edition with an extract from the German version. The German version of the article has been translated from the English version into German. The applicant was ordered to undergo another examination as to his ability to perform military service pursuant to section 24(8) of the Military Service Act (Wehrgesetz), as in force at the relevant time. The applicant appealed against that order, claiming in particular that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. On 26 March 1998 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungs-gerichtshof) dismissed the applicant's complaint. On 14 May 1998 the Lower Austrian Military Authority issued another conscription order for an examination of the applicant’s fitness to perform military service. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. He submitted in particular that by virtue of the 1998 Act, the Jehovah's Witnesses had been granted the status of a “registered religious community’. However, the ten-year period for a successful application for recognition under the Recognition Act (Anerkennungsgesetz) lacked objective justification, he argued. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. Subsequently, the applicant filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted.

The Lublin District Court dissolved the co‑ownership of the building on 10 October 2002 and the applicant and other co-owners appealed against the decision.
